title: What the homepage has to prove for a creative studio
excerpt: Show one decision in the work and a way to start a project. A reel with no explanation loses the client who has already seen fifty portfolios.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall, the way a homepage has to connect one decision to a way to start.
caption: String between screens, one decision tied to the next. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a studio homepage show?
faqs.answer: One decision from real work, the frame that proves it, and a way to start a project. A reel, a slogan, and a logo wall do not do this job. If a stranger cannot repeat the decision in about ten seconds, the first screen is not finished.

faqs.question: How many projects belong on the homepage?
faqs.answer: One project that matches the clients you want next, captioned with the choice. A second project can sit lower if it shows a different kind of decision. An unexplained montage of everything you have made asks the buyer to do your editing.

faqs.question: What should the homepage refuse?
faqs.answer: Awards you cannot explain, client logos that do not open onto work, fake scarcity, and a process diagram with a dozen identical steps. Those blocks reassure the team. They read as wallpaper to a client who has already seen many portfolios.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A creative studio homepage has one job for a client who has already seen fifty portfolios: show one decision in the work, and offer a way to start a project. Taste is not the scarce thing. Judgment is.

A reel with no explanation fails this buyer. They have already watched motion, type, and color. They are looking for the moment someone chose, and for a clear way to ask you to choose again.

## What the first screen has to do

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) on page visits is blunt about the opening. Users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. To earn several minutes of attention, the page has to communicate its value within about 10 seconds. The average visit lasts a little less than a minute, and people read only about a quarter of the text on the pages they do open. Those figures are from a study of ordinary web behavior, not from a studio audience, and they still describe the person who lands on your work.

For this buyer the value is not a slogan about craft. It is one decision they can see. The first screen should carry a sentence a stranger can repeat, the piece of work that proves it, and a way to start a project. If any of those three is missing, the other two cannot save the visit.

Write the sentence in the language of the job, not the language of the mood. "We rebuilt a heritage archive so a reader could find a single engraving without a tour of the institution" is a decision. "We craft digital experiences" is a mood. The client who has sat through fifty portfolios has heard the mood. They stay for the decision.

Keep the first screen short enough to read on a phone without scrolling past the point. A headline, two lines, one image of the work, one action. The rest of the page can earn the longer visit. It cannot earn the first ten seconds if the first screen is a film.

## Name one decision

Pick a project you can explain without a preface. Say what was constrained, what you chose, and what changed for the person using the thing. Then stop. A homepage that tries to prove range before it proves judgment asks the visitor to do your editing.

Public work is a useful model of specificity, even when the studio is not yours. Thomas Bewick is an editorial heritage site: the decision is how a craft archive becomes a place to read, not a museum brochure. Down the Cove is an ecommerce migration and redesign: the decision is what the store keeps so checkout still makes sense. Wabisabi is a calm, tactile world: the decision is restraint, visible in crop and material. Ballarat Box Sports is a community brand with a point of view a local team can recognize. None of these pages would work as an unexplained montage.

You do not need four projects on the first screen. You need one that matches the clients you want next. If you want cultural work, lead with the archive. If you want stores, lead with the migration. Range can live one scroll down, still captioned. Uncaptioned range looks like a reel.

The decision should be checkable. A visitor who opens the project should see the choice in the type, the grid, or the flow, not only in the paragraph. If the sentence claims a cut and the pictures show every option you considered, the sentence is advertising.

## Put the work beside the sentence

The image and the sentence are one argument. Crop to the part that holds the decision. A full-bleed photograph of a studio wall, or a looping film of hands and screens, can be beautiful and still leave the buyer unsure what you did. Caption the frame. "The product grid went from forty tiles to twelve so the material could be read" tells them where to look.

Sequence matters. Decision, then evidence, then a second project only if it shows a different kind of choice. Three projects that all say "we like type" are one project repeated. Two projects that show a brand system and a checkout are a practice.

Do not make the visitor hunt for the work in a modal, a password page, or a PDF. The client who has already seen fifty portfolios will not request a password to discover whether you can choose. If a piece is under embargo, use another piece. Proof that cannot be opened is a claim.

A short line under the work can name the role you played. Design, build, or both. Hanabi designs and builds, so a case can say that the interface and the production front end were one engagement. Say the true scope. Do not imply you shipped the engineering if you handed over frames.

## A way to start a project

The action on the page should say what happens next. "Start a project" is a job. "Learn more" is a delay. Put that action on the first screen and again after the work, where the buyer has just seen the decision and is ready to ask for one.

Say what the next step is in a single sentence near the action. An intro conversation. A short note about the work they need. A link to a page that lists what an engagement includes. The buyer should not have to guess whether you want a brief, a budget, or a moodboard.

Do not ask for the whole project on the homepage. A form with ten fields is a second website. The homepage offers the path. The contact page, if you have one, explains timing and what to have ready. Splitting those jobs keeps the first screen readable.

If you are hiring a studio to make this page, the brief is the same shape as the page. Name the client you want, the decision you want to lead with, and the sentence that starts a project. [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) cover that kind of marketing site: the interface, the front end, and the brand system the page has to obey.

## How much text to keep

People will not read the essay on the homepage. Nielsen Norman Group's finding that visitors read about a quarter of the text is the editing rule. Write the quarter you need them to see, and cut the rest. Short paragraphs. One idea each. A list only when they are choosing or checking.

A useful homepage list is small:

- The kind of client you take.
- The kind of work you do not take.
- The one action that starts a project.

That list is more honest than a paragraph of adjectives. It also gives a skeptical buyer a reason to stay past the first ten seconds, because they can test themselves against it.

The title of the page can be plainer than the headline. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for titles that are descriptive and concise, unique to the page, and free of piled-up phrases. Let the visible headline be the decision. Let the title say what the studio does and for whom. Do not paste the same slogan into both and call it consistency.

Internal pages can carry the longer argument. The homepage points at them. A proof page for a single project, a services page in the buyer's words, a pricing page that shows the shape of the cost. The homepage is the door, not the archive.

## What to leave off

Leave off the reel that has no sentence under it. Leave off an award row you cannot explain in one line. Leave off a client logo wall that does not open onto work. Leave off a process diagram with twelve identical steps. Leave off "full service" as a category. A client who has seen fifty portfolios treats those blocks as wallpaper.

Leave off fake scarcity. "Two spots left this month" on a studio site reads as a template, unless it is literally true and you are willing to say what happens in month two. The page should feel calm. Urgency is not a substitute for a decision.

Leave off a second visual language. If the work is quiet, the homepage chrome should be quiet. Motion can help a transition. It should not be the proof. On a Hanabi site, motion is there to clarify, and reduced motion is part of the build, not a patch at the end. The same standard belongs on a studio homepage: if the animation is the only thing that explains the work, the work is not explained.

## After the homepage

Once the first screen can survive a skeptical client, the next page they open is usually the cost. They are not doing arithmetic yet. They are asking whether a project like the one you showed is a shape they can buy. The [pricing page for a creative studio](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-creative-studio) is the piece to write next, because a decision with no shape of price sends the serious buyer back to guessing.

Build the homepage in the order the buyer uses it. Sentence, work, action. Then the second project. Then the short list of what you take. Read it on a phone before you add anything. If the decision is still visible in ten seconds, the page is ready to design in detail. If it is not, another section will not fix it.
